chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'a, from more than one (narrator), from Aban, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two (peace be upon them both):
regarding the Words of God, Mighty and Majestic: '[Take] the dyeing of God; and who is better than God in dyeing?'
He said: 'The dyeing — it is Islam.'
And he said regarding His Words, Mighty and Majestic: 'Whoever disbelieves in the taghut and believes in God, he has grasped the Firmest Handle.'

key_terms.الطَّاغُوت: Taghut: any false deity, tyrant, or authority that oversteps its bounds and demands obedience in place of God
key_terms.الْعُرْوَة الْوُثْقَى: Al-'urwat al-wuthqa: 'The Firmest Handle' — the most secure bond of faith, here interpreted as iman (true belief)
key_terms.صِبْغَة: Sibgha: dyeing/coloring — in this context, the spiritual 'coloring' or immersion in Islam, possibly referring to the Christian practice of baptism that the Quran responds to

ai.seo_question: What does the Quran mean by 'the dyeing of God' (sibghat Allah) in verse 2:138?
ai.summary: This hadith presents the exegesis of Imam al-Baqir or al-Sadiq (peace be upon them) on two Quranic verses. The first, Quran 2:138, uses the metaphor of 'sibgha' (dyeing/coloring) — in pre-Islamic Arabia, Christians would baptize new converts with colored water as a symbol of purification. The Imam interprets this divine 'dyeing' as Islam itself: the complete immersion of a person in God's religion. The second verse (2:256), with its image of the 'Firmest Handle' (al-'urwat al-wuthqa), is explained as iman (faith) — the unbreakable bond of belief that connects the believer to God when they reject false authorities.
